sentences.text: Noasaurus was a small theropod dinosaur.
The only known species of Noasaurus is Noasaurus leali.
The holotype specimen — the specimen the species is based on — of Noasaurus measures between 1.6 and 2 meters in length.
Gregory S. Paul estimated Noasaurus to be 1.5 meters long and weigh 15 kilograms.
A 2024 study estimated Noasaurus lengths of 1.6 meters and 2 meters based on skull and metatarsal dimensions.
The skull anatomy of Noasaurus is poorly known because only a left maxilla and a right quadrate are preserved.
Noasaurus possessed ziphodont teeth that were laterally compressed, recurved, and serrated on both edges.
Noasaurus likely had a long, S-shaped neck based on comparisons with related dinosaurs and the elongation of its known neck bones.
Curved claws initially thought to be foot claws were later identified as belonging to the forelimbs, resembling those of spinosaurids.
A cervical vertebra found at the site was initially identified in 1999 as oviraptorosaurian, suggesting a rare presence of that group in Gondwana.
In 2007, that same vertebra was re-identified as belonging to Noasaurus.
In April 1975, an expedition led by Professor José F. Bonaparte set out to find fossils in the El Brete area of Salta Province.
The holotype specimen PVL 4061 was discovered in 1975 in the Lecho Formation of Southern Salta by a team led by José Fernando Bonaparte.
Recovered materials included remains of at least five sauropod individuals, including the titanosaur Saltasaurus loricatus.
The species Noasaurus leali was formally described in 1980.
Noasaurus leali was named and described by Bonaparte and Powell in 1980.
Noasaurus was described as a fossil taxon in 1980.
The genus Noasaurus was established by Bonaparte and Powell in 1980.
The species Noasaurus leali was named by Bonaparte and Powell in 1980.
Researchers suggest Noasaurus was an opportunistic mesopredator that likely fed on small vertebrates and fish.
Noasaurus was likely an opportunistic mid-sized predator that fed on small vertebrates like fish.
Researchers suggest the hand claw may have been used to catch fish, a trait convergent with spinosaurids like Baryonyx.
In 2004, one of the hand claws was re-identified as belonging to the hand rather than the foot.
Noasaurus was originally described in 1980 as a coelurosaur and placed in its own family, Noasauridae, which is now classified within Ceratosauria.
Noasaurus is currently classified as a member of the Ceratosauria.
Bonaparte and Powell originally assigned Noasaurus to its own family, the Noasauridae.
Noasaurus is currently considered a member of the Ceratosauria.
Noasaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 70 to 68 million years ago.
Noasaurus lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 70 million years ago between the Campanian and Maastrichtian stages, in what is now South America.
The environment where Noasaurus lived was a coastal plain with ponds and lagoons that likely supported a tropical coastal forest.
Noasaurus lived in a hot, humid environment likely near the Tropic of Capricorn.
Noasaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
There was a debate over whether the large curved claws belonged to the feet or hands, with later studies confirming they were hand claws.
In 1988, Paul hypothesized that noasaurines were South American counterparts of dromaeosaurids through convergent evolution, a view later undermined by the discovery that the claws were on the hands.

Paul hypothesized that Noasaurus might have used a kicking technique to disembowel prey due to short forelimbs, assuming it used foot claws like dromaeosaurids, but this was disproven when the claws were identified as hand claws.
In 2024, Hendrickx et al. placed Noasaurus in a polytomy with other small noasaurids, suggesting a radiation of small-bodied forms during the Late Cretaceous.
